newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy budget to avoid health, pension cuts -press.
newsitem.headline: Italy budget to avoid health, pension cuts -press.

text.p: The forthcoming Italian mini-budget will avoid any cuts to health or pensions spending and will be largely based on accounting changes, Italian newspapers reported on Saturday.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government said on Friday that the package, to be unveiled by the end of the month, would cut between 15-16 trillion lire from the public administration deficit to contain an expected overshoot in 1997 spending.

Financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore said some six trillion lire of this money would be raised by transferring severance payment funds out of companies' accounts and into state coffers. Other dailies said this measure would raise up to seven trillion lire.

Quoting informed sources at the finance ministry, Il Sole said the government would not hike taxes but was planning to accelerate tax payments as well as introduce a fresh crackdown against fiscal fraud.
These measures would raise 4.5 trillion lire, it said.
Other newspapers said the government was still considering increasing value added tax on certain goods.
Most papers reported that plans to impose a one-off tax on people who took early retirement and the introduction of new charges for certain hospital treatment, had both been dropped.
Communist Refoundation, which holds the balance of power in the lower house of parliament, has repeatedly said it will block any new taxes or cuts to welfare spending.
La Stampa newspaper said that Refoundation "would probably accept" the new budget plans.
"It is less certain that (Bank of Italy) governor Antonio Fazio will feel sufficiently re-assured to lower the discount rate," the Turin-based daily said.
Other money might be raised by blocking the transfer of funds to state organisations, such as the post office and state railways, and also cutting back on transfers to the regions.

The Treasury said it would introduce corrective budget measures after latest first quarter data pointed to the deficit ballooning to 76 trillion lire, or 3.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), in 1997.

The government has pledged to bring the deficit/GDP ratio down to three percent this year to meet one of the criteria laid down in the Maastricht treaty for countries wishing to sign up to the planned single European currency.
The mini-budget is expected to be unveiled next Thursday or Friday.
